prompt: At Walter Whitman Middle School, to celebrate the last day of school, Mrs. Hanks brought in treats for her class. She has chocolate bars, lollipops and gumballs. Mrs. Hanks tells each student they can choose any combination of three treats from what she has. How many different combinations of three treats can one of her students choose?

solutions.title: List by type
solutions.body:
Call the treats A, B, C.
- All different: ABC — 1.
- All the same: AAA, BBB, CCC — 3.
- Two of one, one of another: AAB, AAC, BBA, BBC, CCA, CCB — 6.

Total $1 + 3 + 6 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

solutions.title: Stars and bars
solutions.body:
Choosing 3 treats from 3 types with repetition allowed: $\binom{3 + 3 - 1}{3} = \binom53 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

prompt: At the end-of-year assembly, WWMS holds a raffle, in which several lucky students will each win a gift certificate to the famous Giorgio's Gelato. There are 10 gift certificates to be raffled to the 6th graders, 15 gift certificates to be raffled to the 7th graders and 20 gift certificates to be raffled to the 8th graders. Each grade has 300 students. Junie is in 8th grade at WWMS. Junie's sister and brother also attend WWMS and are in 7th and 6th grade, respectively. What is the probability that at least one of the three siblings wins a gift certificate? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Complement
solutions.body:
Each grade's certificates go to different students, so the 6th-grade brother wins with probability $\frac{10}{300} = \frac1{30}$, the 7th-grade sister with $\frac{15}{300} = \frac1{20}$, and Junie with $\frac{20}{300} = \frac1{15}$. The three raffles are separate, so the events are independent.

$P(\text{nobody wins}) = \frac{29}{30} \cdot \frac{19}{20} \cdot \frac{14}{15} = \frac{7714}{9000}$.

$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - \frac{7714}{9000} = \frac{1286}{9000} = \frac{643}{4500} \approx 0.143$.

(Simply adding $\frac1{30} + \frac1{20} + \frac1{15} = \frac{3}{20}$ counts the cases where two or three of them win more than once.)

**Answer: $\frac{643}{4500}$**

reviewNote: The official solution gives 3/20 by adding 1/30 + 1/20 + 1/15, which double-counts outcomes where two or three siblings win (the events are not mutually exclusive). The correct probability 1 - (29/30)(19/20)(14/15) = 643/4500 is used here; a human should confirm.

prompt: Before WWMS students were officially released for summer vacation, the staff had to conduct an official check of all 900 lockers, numbered from 1 to 900. Once the locker check was completed, all 900 lockers remained open. As students exited in an orderly fashion, walking down the hallway single file, the 1st student closed all the lockers. The 2nd student then opened every even numbered locker. The 3rd student changed the status of every locker whose number was a multiple of three – opened it if closed or closed it if opened. The 4th student then did the same for every locker whose number was a multiple of four, and so on through the 900th student who changed the status of locker number 900. When all of the students had left the school, how many lockers were closed?

solutions.title: Count the toggles
solutions.body:
Locker $n$ is toggled once by each student whose number divides $n$. Starting open, it ends closed after an odd number of toggles, i.e. when $n$ has an odd number of divisors. Divisors pair up ($d$ with $n/d$) except when $d = n/d$, so only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors. The squares from 1 to 900 are $1^2, 2^2, \dots, 30^2$: **30** lockers.

**Answer: 30**

solutions.title: Small case check
solutions.body:
Try lockers 1–10: locker 1 (divisor 1) closed; 2 (1,2) open; 3 open; 4 (1,2,4) closed; 5–8 open; 9 (1,3,9) closed; 10 open. Closed lockers are 1, 4, 9 — the squares. Up to 900 there are 30 squares.

**Answer: 30**
